New SEMs can handle large samples with great ease
 Latest electron microscopes from Hitachi High-Technologies allow researchers to observe large samples with superior automatic function

Scanning electron microscopes are an essential and powerful tool, but researchers are sometimes frustrated when it comes to working with automobile parts and other large, heavy objects. SEM operators are usually required to prepare samples for observation by cutting them into pieces to fit the chamber. This also limits the use of conventional SEMs for some academic applications, such as archaeological samples, which cannot be damaged. SEMs largely rely on an operator’s skills to adjust images and maintain the instrument condition, so it can be difficult to acquire consistently high-quality data.
In April 2019, Hitachi High-Technologies, one of the world’s major SEM manufacturers, released two models in a bid to overcome these obstacles, and improve laboratory efficiencies.
The SU3800 responds to user requests for automation.© Hitachi High-Technologies
“Both the SU3800 and the SU3900 are a response to growing requests for automation and large chambers, from both industrial engineers and academic researchers,” says Masanari Furiki, a Hitachi High-Technologies product manager engaged in the development of these two models. The SU3900 has a large chamber that accommodates a sample measuring 300 mm in diameter, 130 mm in height and weighing 5 kg — 2.5 times more capacity than the previous SEM models. Images can be magnified up to 800,000 times in both models.
“Using the SU3900, researchers can mount a large bulk sample such as grindstone, cutting tools, automobile components or control boards without cutting, and observe as they are,” adds Tatsuya Hirato, chief engineer of the SEMs. For example, the user can put a drill bit in the chamber and easily make a comparison of how the drill tip changes before and after use.
The SU3900 can accommodate large samples.© Hitachi High-Technologies
Both the SU3800 and the SU3900 feature user-friendly automated functions to minimize human error and realize the machine’s best possible performance. “We reconsidered and enhanced the algorithms of auto adjustment functions for image acquisition such as the optical alignment to enable users to acquire high-quality data at a high speed,” Hirato says.
The controls of the SU3800 and the SU3900 allow intuitive moving to the desired position by clicking the mouse on the image with the chamber’s built-in camera. The lens can be zoomed in and out from the optical image magnification to the SEM image magnification seamlessly by stitching multiple images. Prompt observation can improve the researcher’s efficiency. “These new functions enable the user to move the observation position smoothly by utilizing a mapping application software,” Hirato says.
The new microscopes also realize efficient X-ray or micro analysis and improved throughput thanks to complementary support systems. The latest EDS integration system unifies operations of all processes from stage location and setting up for analysis, through to measurement and reporting, allowing the user to control operations from the microscope’s graphic user interface.
Hitachi High-Technologies spent two years developing the SU3800 and the SU3900 by solving difficulties in the development of electronic optical systems, stages and samples. The biggest headache, Hirato says, was downsizing high-voltage power sources, while maintaining the performance of discharging and stability. The engineers overhauled specifications of insulating materials and components from scratch and found optimal solutions for each issue.
Tatsuya Hirato (front right) and Masanari Furiki (far right, second back row), and their team, with the SU3900 model, whose chamber capacity is 2.5 times that of previous models.© Hitachi High-Technologies
Global demand for SEMs is steadily growing, but their use varies by region. Demand for large-chamber microscopes is especially rising in North America, while compact-sized machines are needed across the world. For models of any size, improved automation is the most attractive function for users, Furiki says.
“Having released two models at the same time, we believe we can provide a great cost performance and wonderful experiences of SEM observations for both inexperienced and advanced users,” Hirato says.
